Yes, under Nigerian law, you can assign copyright in your song to a label for a limited period rather than permanently. This is stated in s.19(3), which allows for an assignment of copyright "for a limited period."
Yes, under Nigerian law, when you die, your copyright in your books can pass to your children under your will, as stated in s.36(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022.

According to s.25(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, a non-profit library or other non-profit institution established in Nigeria for the purpose of providing reading facilities or materials to persons with disabilities may make or procure a copy of any work from which copies may be made under this section, if the work is available in an appropriate format only through commercial exploitation. However, this provision does not require the consent of the owner of the copyright in the work or a licence from them.

Yes, under Nigerian law, a blind reader in Kano who has lawfully bought an ebook is allowed to convert it into a format her screen reader can handle for her own use, as stated in s.13(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022.

Yes, as per s.13(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, you may make an audio version of the work for him if he is a person with a physical disability and has lawfully acquired a copy of the work in its original form.

Yes, it may send them, as stated in s.25(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, which allows a non-profit organisation established in Nigeria for the benefit of people with disabilities to make or procure copies of a work available to persons with such disability if they have no reason to believe that the copy will be used by anyone other than the person concerned.

s.114 states that it is permissible for a service provider to remove or disable any technology, product, service, device, component, or part that is used in an infringement of copyright under this Act, provided that such action is taken in good faith and is not more restrictive than necessary to achieve that purpose. This indicates that there are provisions for technological protection measures, but they must be balanced with the rights of copyright owners and the public interest.

s.112 states that "it shall be permissible for any person to make or procure a licence for the use of any technological protection measure." This implies that under this section, there is a potential for licensing agreements related to software, as it allows for the creation or acquisition of a license for the use of such measures.

Yes, section 110 of the Copyright Act 2022 deals with orphan works. The procedure outlined in subsection (1) states that where an owner of copyright in a work cannot be identified or located after reasonable effort, the work shall be treated as an orphan work and may be dealt with by the person who first makes available to the public a copy of the work. Subsection (2) specifies that any person dealing with an orphan work shall not be liable for infringement of copyright under this Act if they did not have actual knowledge that the work was an orphan work and acted reasonably and in good faith.

Section 118 of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022 states that no person shall be liable for any infringement of copyright in a database if the alleged infringer did not have actual knowledge that the use of the material was an infringement of copyright and where reasonable efforts have been made to determine the identity of the alleged infringer. This provision aims to balance the protection of copyright owners with the need to prevent undue burden on service providers. 

Cited as: s.118.

Section 125 of the Copyright Act 2022 prescribes the following penalties for online piracy:

(a) A fine of at least N1,000,000 or imprisonment for a term of at least five years for an individual and a fine of at least N5,000,000 for a body corporate; and  
(b) A fine of at least N5,000,000 or imprisonment for a term of at least ten years for an individual and a fine of at least N20,000,000 for a body corporate. 

This is stated in s.46(3).

s.111 states that "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Act, copyright in a work created by an artificial intelligence shall vest in the entity that commissioned or procured the creation of the work." This implies that the creator of the artificial intelligence, not the AI itself, holds the copyright.

s.120 states that the resale royalty shall apply to any sale of an original work of art by or on behalf of the author, where the selling price is at least equal to the published negotiated price for similar works of the same category as determined by the Commission.

s.115 states that an owner of copyright in a work may authorise the importation into Nigeria of copies of the work from any country where the work is not available through general trade or where there is no authorised distribution system for the work. This is subject to the provisions of section 114 of the Act. 

Additionally, s.115 allows for the export from Nigeria of such copies to any country where they are not available through general trade or where there is no authorised distribution system for the work, provided that the export is not for commercial purposes and is accompanied by a declaration to that effect. 

It also specifies that the importation or export of any copy of a work shall be deemed to be with the consent of the copyright owner if the work has been imported or exported under this section. 

Furthermore, s.115 grants the Commission the power to prescribe conditions for the importation or export of works under this section, including the imposition of a levy on the importation or export of such works. 

Lastly, it provides that the provisions of this section shall not apply to works which are subject to a licensing scheme approved under section 87 of the Act. 

In summary, s.115 enables the importation and export of works that are not available through general trade or have no authorised distribution system, subject to certain conditions and limitations.

Yes, under Nigerian law, section 113 of the Copyright Act 2022 creates a right for film extras and background performers. This is indicated in subsection (1) which states that "an author of an audiovisual work is entitled to share in the proceeds of any distribution of copies of the audiovisual work." This implies that performers, including extras and background performers, are included as authors in this context.

s.130 states that copyright shall not subsist in an arrangement of text or illustrations in any work if the arrangement consists solely of the direction of character shapes and strokes and is without artistic or aesthetic quality. This implies that while copyright exists in other aspects of typography, the specific arrangement described does not qualify for protection under this provision.

Section 104A of the Copyright Act 2022 provides that in any proceeding for an infringement of copyright under this Act, it shall be presumed that there is an infringement of copyright if the defendant is found to have an article or other subject matter in his possession or control which is known or has been known to be an infringing copy or an article capable of making an infringing copy. This presumption can be rebutted by proof to the contrary. (s.104A)

s.296(b) states that "circumvention of any technological protection measure" is covered under this section. Therefore, it refers to actions taken to bypass or overcome technological protections designed to prevent unauthorized access to copyrighted works.

Yes, under s.97(a) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, the court may order the service provider to expeditiously disclose to the owner of copyright or their agent, information sufficient to identify the alleged infringer. Additionally, under s.97(b), the court may issue an order that the service provider shall expeditiously take down or disable access to the material that is claimed to be infringing or to be the subject of infringing activity. These provisions collectively empower the court to grant injunctions against service providers in appropriate circumstances.

s.31A. Copies for persons with disability.—(a) A person with a disability may make or procure a copy of a work from which he is unable to gain access by reason of visual or auditory impairment, if the copy is not available in any other format and is required solely for the purpose of accessing the work; and (b) A person with a disability may make or procure a copy of a work from which he is unable to gain access by reason of physical or mental disability, if the copy is not available in any other format and is required solely for the purpose of accessing the work.

s.73B provides for the payment of royalties to owners of copyright in works transmitted by means of a satellite or cable system. Specifically, it states that the Commission shall pay such royalties as may be determined by regulations made under this Act, subject to any agreement between the Commission and an owner of copyright in a work dealt with under this section.

s.19(4) states that copyright in a database is conferred only if there is an effective arrangement for the owner to control the making available to the public of copies of the database by wire or wireless means in such a way as to constitute a reprographic copying of the whole or a substantial part of the database. Therefore, it implies that copyright in a database lasts as long as the arrangements for controlling the making available to the public of copies of the database continue.

s.4(2) states that it is permissible for the Commission to require any person or entity to deposit any work with them, as they may deem fit. This indicates that there is a potential for deposit requirements, but their necessity and specifics would be determined by the Commission's discretion.
s.103(2) states that any appeal against a judgment or order of the court under this section shall be to the Court of Appeal.

s.88(12) states that a foreign collective management organisation shall not be recognised under this Act if it is not approved by the Commission or if its activities in Nigeria are inconsistent with the objectives of this Act. This implies that while there is a provision for recognition, there are conditions that must be met before an approval can be granted.

s.74(8) states that an expression of folklore shall not be eligible for registration under this Act if it is or includes any element which is— (a) an expression of folklore which has been subject to protection by way of any other form of intellectual property right; or (b) an expression of folklore which is or includes an element which is or includes an expression of folklore which has been subject to protection by way of any other form of intellectual property right.
Section 61(2) of the Copyright Act 2022 states that any person dissatisfied with the order made under subsection (1) may appeal against the order to the Court of Appeal.

s.36(5) states that an online service provider shall not be liable for monetary relief for infringement of copyright under this section if they meet certain conditions, including promptly suspending or disabling access to the content upon obtaining actual knowledge of the infringing activity.
s.9(3) states that the right to control the rental of literary or musical works is not included in the rights conferred by this Act.
s.19(1)(f) states that copyright in a computer program shall last for 50 years commencing from the year in which it was first made available to the public or published.

s.2(1)(g) states "audiovisual works." Therefore, section 2(1)(g) adds audiovisual works to the list of works eligible for copyright under this Act.

s.3(d) states that "procedures for fixing or reproducing an idea or system" are not eligible for copyright under this Act.

Section 54(2)(g) of the Copyright Act 2022 requires that the service provider shall include in its notification to the subscriber or account holder, a link to the content or an identification of the content which is claimed to infringe copyright under this section. 

Cited as: s.54(2)(g).

Section 88(2)(e) of the Copyright Act 2022 requires that a collective management organisation seeking approval must have a minimum of three members who are qualified in copyright matters and at least one member from each of the following categories: persons with disabilities, women, youth, persons with physical or sensory disabilities, and persons from rural communities.

To file a copyright application with the Nigerian Copyright Registration Authority, you must submit the prescribed fee to the Director-General or any other designated officer of the Commission. The processing time for the application is three months from the date of receipt. (s.48)

The role of the Copyright Tribunal of Nigeria in resolving licensing disputes is to arbitrate and determine any dispute arising from the operation of a scheme for the regulation of the granting of licences by way of compulsory licensing of copyright works (s.89(1)).
To appeal a decision under Nigerian law, you must apply in writing to the National Court of Nigeria for leave to appeal against the judgment or order. This is outlined in s.100(1).

Yes, under Nigerian law, your work is automatically covered once it is entered in the National Register of Creative Works. This is stated in s.48(1)(a), which specifies that "the work shall be deemed to have been registered."
The Nigerian Copyright Regulations 1999 require that an assignment of copyright must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the author, as stated in s.34(2).

Yes, under Nigerian law, the Copyright Enforcement Directorate has power to seize infringing goods at the border. This is stated in s.83(1)(b), which grants the Director-General the authority to inspect any property or goods at the point of entry into Nigeria for the purpose of ascertaining whether they are works protected by this Act and to seize any such work or other contrivance if there is reasonable cause to suspect that it is an infringing work.

The duration of protection for your musical works under this Act is as follows:

- For a work first published after 31 December 1964, it shall be protected until 75 years after the end of the year in which the work was created or 75 years after the year of its first publication, whichever is later.
- For a work first published before 31 December 1964, it shall be protected until 70 years after the end of the year in which the work was created or 70 years after the year of its first publication, whichever is later.

This is outlined in s.6(1).

According to s.23(1) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, a non-profit educational institution may make copies of any literary or musical work by means of a reprographic process in respect of current courses of instruction, provided that:  
(a) the copying is not more than one copy in ten percent of the total number of copies of the work issued by the publisher;  
(b) the work is available only in an original form; and  
(c) the copies made shall be retained by the institution and shall not be sold or rented to members of the public.  

Therefore, your department can legally copy materials for students as long as these conditions are met.

According to s.19(1) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, copyright in literary or musical works can be transferred by way of assignment or licence. It is important for you to understand that this transfer can be done during the creation of the work or at any time thereafter, as stated in s.19(2). Additionally, it is noted that copyright cannot be transferred by operation of law, as per s.19(3). Therefore, before signing your first publishing deal, you should consider these provisions carefully and ensure that you are comfortable with the terms of any transfer that may occur.

According to s.45 of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, an infringement of the rights conferred by sections 10 and 11 of the Act constitutes an offence under the Copyright Act and is actionable in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Specifically, s.46 states that any person who does or causes any person to do any of the acts specified in subsection (1) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of at least N100,000 or imprisonment for a term of at least one year or both. 

In terms of relief, s.47 provides that the court may award damages, injunction, and account of profits or conversion to the owner of the copyright. Therefore, before proceeding to a lawyer, you can seek damages, injunction, and orders for accounts of profits or conversion from the court.

You have to comply with the conditions set out in regulations made by the Commission under this section, which include measures such as monitoring, taking down or disabling links to infringing content, and notifying users regarding their rights management information (s.54(1)). You become liable for infringing material uploaded by users if you are not acting expeditiously to remove or disable access to the material after becoming aware or having reasonable grounds to suspect that it is being used in violation of the Act (s.54(2)).

According to s.6(a) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, a performer has the exclusive right to control the fixation of their performance, which includes having the right to determine where and when the fixation shall take place. Additionally, under s.6(b), a performer is entitled to share in any payment received by the person who arranges for the fixation of their performance with them as an author. Therefore, you have the rights to control the fixation of your performance and to receive a share in any payment related to the arrangement for its fixation.

s.10(1)(b) states that folklore and related cultural expressions, including oral traditions, musical works, dance forms, and dramatic works are eligible for protection under this Act. Therefore, your family's community has traditional songs that could potentially receive protection under this provision.

To start a royalty collection body for Nigerian producers, the law requires that the body must be incorporated as a company limited by guarantee and must be registered under the Companies and Allied Matters Act, as stated in s.87(1). Additionally, it must be approved by the Commission, as outlined in s.87(2).

The levy on copying equipment in Nigeria is referred to as the "copying device levy" and is imposed by the Commission. It applies to any person who imports, sells, distributes, or possesses for commercial purposes any copying device, which is capable of making copies of literary or musical works without the authorisation of the owner of the copyright (s.89(1)). The payment of this levy is mandatory and must be made directly to the Commission (s.89(2)).

According to s.23(1) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, you may make and use any equipment or contrivances for the purpose of making copies of any work from which an infringing copy has been made, if the work is available in that format in the collection of the library. Additionally, under s.23(2), you may reproduce any such work in the course of instruction or research, provided that the reproduction is not by means of a reprographic process and is not sold or let for hire.

As a blind reader in Nigeria, you and organisations serving you are allowed to make or procure a copy of any published literary or musical work in any format that is accessible to people with visual disabilities, if the work has not been made available to the public by means of sale or other transfer of ownership. This is stated in s.8(1)(a). Additionally, you may reproduce or cause to be reproduced any such work in an accessible format, as per s.8(1)(b). Furthermore, you are permitted to distribute to persons with visual disabilities copies of such works in accessible formats, as outlined in s.8(1)(c).

Registration of a work with the Copyright Commission provides several benefits to the owner, as outlined in s.43:

1. **Proof of Ownership**: Registration serves as prima facie proof of the ownership of the work (s.43(a)).
2. **Notice of Work**: It informs the public that the work has been registered (s.43(b)).
3. **Notice of Owner**: It notifies the owner that their work is registered (s.43(c)).
4. **Presumption of Eligibility**: It presumes that the name appearing on the work is that of the owner (s.43(d)).
5. **Presumption of Authorship**: It presumes that the author named on the work is the owner (s.43(e)).

These provisions help protect the rights of the creator and ensure that they receive recognition and potential financial benefits from their creative efforts.

Yes, you have a route open to you as per s.36(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, which states that the Commission may authorise or grant permission for the translation of a work if it is in the interest of the public to do so.

Copyright in a work created by a person in the course of employment shall vest in that person unless there is an agreement to the contrary (s.19(1)(a)). In the absence of such an agreement, copyright shall vest in the employer (s.19(1)(b)). Therefore, if you are commissioned to take photographs as part of your job, copyright will likely vest in you. However, if there is an express agreement between you and your client stating otherwise, then the ownership would be determined accordingly.
Yes, you may have additional rights beyond the copyright you already sold, as you can claim infringement of your right to honour or reputation under s.14(1)(b) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022.

Yes, apart from suing the seller, you can apply to the court for an order that the site hosting the infringing content be blocked or removed. This is stated in s.54(1)(b), which allows for an application to the court for an order that "the site hosting the infringing content be blocked or removed."

According to s.103(1) of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, you are entitled to an award of damages, injunction, or both in respect of infringement of any right conferred by this Act. The court may also order the infringing copy or article to be delivered up to you. 

To prove their case, the plaintiff must show that:

(a) they are the owner of the copyright in the work or have the authority to act on behalf of the owner;  
(b) there is an infringement of any right conferred by this Act; and  
(c) it would be inequitable for the defendant to retain the alleged infringing copy or article.

In response, the defendant must demonstrate that they did not know and had no reason to believe that their conduct constituted an infringement of any right conferred by this Act.
